title: Construction Industry and Project Management Basics (PMT 801)
subject: Project management
description: Thirty questions across easy, medium and hard on how the construction industry works, what projects and project management are, the knowledge areas and the project manager's role.

questions.prompt: Which problem does the lecture say its concern is about handling, through real estate construction project management?
options: Building failure, abandonment and collapse of building infrastructure
The rate of borrowing capital to invest
Property taxes and estate duties
Flood and gully erosion affecting demand
questions.explanation: The lecture lists many threats to real estate investors, then says its concern is the threat of building failure, abandonment and collapse, whose solution lies in project management.

questions.prompt: Which definition of a project does Osuagwu (1997) give?
options: A routine activity repeated every year
A permanent organisation with fixed staff
A group of departments sharing one budget
A series of related activities with a goal, a beginning and an end
questions.explanation: The key features are a goal, a start and an end.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a characteristic of a project?
options: It is repetitive and continuous
It always involves only one organisation
A life cycle with a starting point and an ending point
It needs no specific objective
questions.explanation: Projects have a well-articulated aim, a life cycle, a network of time and cost activities, are unique and one-time, may cut across organisations, and may need a special organisation.

questions.prompt: How does Baridam (2002) describe management?
options: Controlling costs and nothing else
Getting things done through and with people
Designing the finished product
Selecting the cheapest contractor
questions.explanation: Baridam sees management as planning and directing effort towards a common objective with and through people.

questions.prompt: According to the PMBOK Guide (2009), what is project management?
options: The supervision of workers on a construction site
A method of choosing between competing investments
The application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities to meet project requirements
The legal process of awarding contracts
questions.explanation: This is the PMBOK definition quoted in the lecture.

questions.prompt: How many knowledge areas must a project manager know, according to the lecture?
options: Nine
Six
Seven
Ten
questions.explanation: There are six core areas, two facilitating areas (communications and risk), and integration management as the ninth.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the six core knowledge areas?
options: Project communication management
Project risk management
Project integration management
Project materials management
questions.explanation: The six core areas are scope, time, cost, quality, materials and human resources management. Communications and risk are facilitating areas, and integration is the ninth.

questions.prompt: Who is described as the person to coordinate the interests and roles of the many professionals on a real estate project?
options: The client
The project manager
The architect
The contractor
questions.explanation: Without someone to coordinate architects, engineers, quantity surveyors, builders and others, the lecture says the result would be disastrous.

questions.prompt: How many distinct stages does construction procedure in Nigeria have, according to the lecture?
options: Two: the design stage and the construction stage
Three: design, tendering and construction
Four: design, tendering, construction and maintenance
One: design and construction together
questions.explanation: Design is separated from construction, unlike manufacturing where the two are integrated.

questions.prompt: Which four main headings does Lock (2004) use to classify projects?
options: Tangible, intangible, commercial and non-commercial projects
New, expansion, updating and rehabilitation projects
Construction and allied, manufacturing, management and research projects
Public, private, joint and community projects
questions.explanation: The other options are different classifications in the lecture: tangible and intangible, motive, and resource commitment.

questions.prompt: How do construction and manufacturing differ in design and production?
options: In construction, design and production are done by one organisation, while in manufacturing they are separated
Both industries separate design from production in the same way
In manufacturing, design teams are appointed from different organisations for each product
In construction, design and execution are done by different organisations, while in manufacturing both are housed in one factory environment
questions.explanation: In construction the design teams are normally appointed from different organisations and the construction team erects what they design.

questions.prompt: Why does construction involve cost prediction risk that manufacturing largely avoids?
options: Construction products are always cheaper to make
In construction the price is set before production, while in manufacturing production is completed before price is attached
Manufacturing prices are fixed by the government
Construction projects avoid competitive tendering
questions.explanation: The contractor must predict costs from the design documents, with the risks and uncertainties that come with that.

questions.prompt: Why is the construction industry described as fragmented?
options: Demand comes from many individual clients with one-off requirements, and supply ranges from jobbing builders to multinationals
A few large clients dominate with identical needs
Only government firms supply construction
All construction firms are about the same size
questions.explanation: The lecture compares it to the car industry making every car to the owner's own specification.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the need for a real estate product is 'derived'?
options: Demand comes only from government
Demand is fixed by seasonal cycles
The desire for it is determined by the demand for the goods and services it helps to create
Demand is copied from other countries
questions.explanation: Together with violent fluctuation from seasonal, cyclical and government action, this makes real estate projects difficult to manage.

questions.prompt: In the traditional construction process, how is the contractor selected?
options: By negotiation before any design starts
By the architect's personal choice during design
By drawing lots among registered firms
By competitive tendering after the design is substantially completed
questions.explanation: The designer then manages the process from inception to completion.

questions.prompt: Why did the traditional method of managing construction fail to meet clients' needs?
options: Clients stopped wanting new buildings
The unstable economic, political, social and technological environment made projects more complex, with many specialists and stakeholders
Local materials became too expensive
Design and construction became too closely integrated
questions.explanation: Stable, simple construction suited the old method, but modern projects are complex and have many stakeholders.

questions.prompt: Which of these describes the turnkey or package deal?
options: A consultant only supervises the work for the client
A contractor is chosen by tender after the design is complete
One organisation is employed by the client to design, construct and equip or furnish the facility
The client designs and builds the facility alone
questions.explanation: The project management approach is a separate innovation, where a project manager is appointed to manage a project from inception to completion.

questions.prompt: Which pair of reports does the lecture name as drivers of change in the construction industry?
options: The Egan Report of 1994 (Constructing the Team) and the Latham Report of 1998 (Rethinking Construction)
The RIBA Report of 1994 and the M4I Report of 1998
The PMBOK Report of 1994 and the PERT Report of 1998
The Latham Report of 1994 (Constructing the Team) and the Egan Report of 1998 (Rethinking Construction)
questions.explanation: Rethinking Construction called for radical change to the processes through which the industry delivers projects.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the first three sequential steps in project management?
options: Determine the duration of tasks, define the objectives, allocate resources
Define the objectives, determine the tasks, decide on important milestones
Allocate resources, decide on milestones, determine the tasks
Decide on milestones, determine the tasks, define the objectives
questions.explanation: The seven steps run: define objectives, determine tasks, decide milestones, determine durations, plan the organisation of tasks, allocate resources, then re-evaluate and carry out the project.

questions.prompt: What does project quality management ensure, according to the knowledge areas section?
options: That the project satisfies the stated or implied needs for which it was undertaken
That the project is finished in the shortest possible time
That the budget is realistic and cost overruns are avoided
That staff are recruited and their time monitored
questions.explanation: It means satisfying the client's taste and the end users' expectations.

questions.prompt: A government hospital has some element of profit alongside other motives. Under the classification by motive, what kind of project is it?
options: Pure commercial
Non-commercial
Quasi-commercial
Intangible
questions.explanation: Pure commercial projects are undertaken for profit only, and quasi-commercial ones combine profit with other motives. Hospitals and educational establishments are the lecture's public sector examples.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of project type and description is correct?
options: Expansion project: establishes a new independent productive establishment
New project: improves the economic performance of existing projects
Rehabilitation project: expands an existing productive entity
Updating project: updates the technology of an existing project without major change in output
questions.explanation: New projects set up financially independent establishments, expansion projects enlarge existing ones, and rehabilitation or maintenance projects improve the economic performance of existing projects.

questions.prompt: Why are research projects described as very high risk?
options: They are expensive in time and money, and may end in a major breakthrough or a complete waste of resources
They are carried out in unpredictable factory environments
They must always be executed on a site away from head office
Their results are always physical items
questions.explanation: The uncertain outcome is what makes research projects risky.

questions.prompt: Why are manufacturing projects said to be less risky than construction projects?
options: They need fewer professionals
Their factory environment is predictable
They are always smaller
They have no deadlines
questions.explanation: Construction projects are executed on sites away from head office and need massive resources.

questions.prompt: What is the main distinctive feature of construction and allied projects?
options: They are conducted in factories with predictable conditions
Their results cannot be measured as hardware
They are occasional undertakings with no physical item
Execution must be done on a site different from the organisation's head office, and resource requirements are massive
questions.explanation: The other options describe manufacturing projects and management projects.

questions.prompt: Which of these is listed as a role of the project manager?
options: Personally producing the structural drawings
Directing and controlling the contractor and sub-contractors to curb excesses, wastage and delays
Choosing the end users of the building
Replacing the client's board of directors
questions.explanation: The project manager's role also includes coordinating the work programme, maintaining quality, liaising with all parties, advising on design, cost, tax and legal matters, and monitoring cash flow.

questions.prompt: How can the project manager attain set goals without sacrificing standards and quality?
options: Through experience in value engineering analysis or value management
By reducing the number of inspections
By refusing any change to the design
By appointing more subcontractors
questions.explanation: The lecture ties this to the manager's advice on design and cost.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the real estate sector does the lecture make?
options: It is stable and steady, like mass production
It supplies only luxury accommodation
It fluctuates violently because of seasonal, cyclical and government action, causing under and over use of capacity
Its products are cheap and easily moved
questions.explanation: The lecture also notes that its products are bulky and expensive.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the seven targets set in the report Rethinking Construction?
options: Scope, time, cost, quality, risk, communication and procurement
Design, materials, labour, equipment, supervision, inspection and maintenance
Prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure, rework, scrap and warranty
Cost, time, predictability, defects, accidents, productivity and turnover or profits
questions.explanation: The report also urged a culture of performance measurement so that innovations could be evaluated and continuous improvement promoted.

questions.prompt: Which of these is among the threats the lecture lists for real estate investors?
options: An excess of skilled labour and cheap materials
The opportunity cost of choosing real estate and the time value of money
Overly stable demand and fixed prices
Unlimited access to cheap credit
questions.explanation: The lecture also lists building failure, where and when to build, environmental challenges, borrowing rates, profit measurement and government policies.
